hero.headline: Proposed homestead exemption expansion could cost Martin County over $67 million
hero.teaser: A Florida homestead exemption expansion on the November ballot could lower tax bills for homeowners but may shift the tax burden to renters if local governments raise rates to offset lost revenue.
hero.body:
A proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could provide tax relief for homeowners, but critics worry the benefit may come at the expense of renters if local governments need to raise rates to compensate for lost revenue. According to analysis from the Florida Policy Institute, Martin County could lose more than $67 million if voters approve the amendment in November. The statewide impact could be even more significant, with local governments across Florida potentially losing nearly $4.8 billion in total revenue.

Mike Readling, executive director of Habitat for Humanity of Martin County, expressed concern that the proposed tax cut would not help the people his organization typically serves. He noted a recent increase in people seeking assistance with rent and bills, with 95 percent being renters. "The housing situation is so dire. It's gotten progressively worse. We have families coming in everyday," Readling said. He believes the exemption would not benefit the demographic his organization works with. Attorney John Tolley explained that local governments facing budget shortfalls would have limited options: reduce services, use reserve funds, or increase millage rates.

Realtor Michael Caputo acknowledged that if millage rates rise, landlords without homestead exemptions could face higher tax bills and potentially pass those costs to renters. However, he noted the amendment would also lower the property tax cap on non-homesteaded properties, including commercial apartment complexes, from 10 percent down to 5 percent. A 2025 Florida Senate analysis found only 24 affordable and available rental units exist for every 100 extremely low-income renters in the state.

Caputo expressed skepticism that municipalities would actually raise millage rates, suggesting the market dynamics might prevent significant rent increases. "If they're paying more for their property, they're going to try and increase that on the tenant and give it a try. If it doesn't happen for them, then they'll have to readjust their pricing," Caputo said. Attorney Tolley added that the lower tax cap on rental properties could potentially lead to reduced rents. Despite these competing perspectives, the core concern remains whether the homestead exemption expansion will ultimately burden renters who do not benefit from the tax break while local governments grapple with reduced revenue.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie distributes $24 million Waste Pro settlement via property tax roll
cards.teaser: Port St.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie city council voted Monday to distribute $24 million from a settlement with former trash hauler Waste Pro through the property tax roll rather than sending out checks. The city selected the tax roll option because it allows funds to be distributed directly to properties via an established system. Council members also voted not to reimburse the city for prior emergency solid waste expenses in the general fund.

The settlement resolved lawsuits filed in 2021 between the city and Waste Pro. The company blamed labor shortages while the city argued the company breached its contract for standard service. Resident Kelly Lee described the problems during the pandemic, noting neighbors experienced trash piling up on their yards when Waste Pro failed to pick it up. Before the vote, Lee raised concerns about fair distribution, questioning how former residents who lived in Port St. Lucie during the service problems but have since moved would receive their share. She also noted that some current residents did not pay into Waste Pro and were not affected by the issues. Scott Samples with the city said staff collected data and created scenarios to provide recommendations to council. Mayor Shannon Martin said in April after the settlement announcement that she wanted to see the cash in residents' pockets and was committed to making sure residents got paid back for what they dealt with during that time.

cards.headline: 18-year-old biking from Jacksonville to Keys missing for days, last seen in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: An 18-year-old who was biking from Jacksonville to the Florida Keys has been missing for several days. He was last seen in Fort Pierce.
cards.body:
An 18-year-old bicyclist traveling from Jacksonville to the Florida Keys has been reported missing after not being seen for several days. The young man was last spotted in Fort Pierce, according to authorities.

The missing person was on a long-distance bicycle journey from Jacksonville in northeast Florida to the Florida Keys when he disappeared. Fort Pierce, located in St. Lucie County, was the last confirmed location where the 18-year-old was seen.

Authorities are seeking information from the public about the missing bicyclist's whereabouts. Anyone who may have seen the 18-year-old or has information about his location is urged to contact law enforcement.

cards.teaser: Port St.

The tax roll option allows the city to distribute funds directly to properties using an established system. The settlement concludes years of trash collection problems in Port St. Lucie. cards.headline: 14-year-old Congress Middle School student killed by speeding driver in Boynton Beach
cards.teaser: Christopher Cetoute, a 14-year-old Congress Middle School student, was fatally struck by a speeding driver on North Congress Avenue in Boynton Beach.
cards.body:
Christopher Cetoute, a 14-year-old student at Congress Middle School, was killed Friday night when struck by a speeding driver along the 4600 block of North Congress Avenue in Boynton Beach. According to Boynton Beach police, Christopher was crossing the roadway going eastbound when he was hit by a 35-year-old driver traveling southbound. Police believe speeding played a factor in the crash. Christopher was not crossing at a crosswalk and was pronounced dead at the scene. No charges have been filed against the driver at this time.

Friends remember Christopher as loyal, hilarious, determined, caring and easy to get close to. Abrionna Lang, a close friend, said "At first I didn't believe it until I'd seen a lot of stuff and then I just started crying. Like I was crying for the whole day." Christopher loved playing basketball and track. Caurline Robinson, who lives in the area, said she has witnessed at least seven crashes along Congress Avenue in the last eight years and is calling for safety enhancements. Robinson lost her 5-year-old great-grandchild to a speeding driver in 2021. A vigil will be held in Christopher's honor Friday at 7 p.m. at the memorial site on North Congress Avenue.

cards.headline: Palm Beach Gardens woman receives repeated toll bills from stolen temporary tag
cards.teaser: Vera Keswick-Paine continues to receive toll bills from Florida's Gulf Coast for a black Mercedes she does not own, after someone stole the temporary tag registered to her husband.
cards.body:
Vera Keswick-Paine of Palm Beach Gardens received a toll bill in March for multiple tolls along Florida's Gulf Coast. The license plate number matched a temporary tag registered to her husband, but the bill referenced a black Mercedes with a photo. The Keswicks drive a white Nissan, which has had a permanent tag for months. Keswick-Paine filed a report with Palm Beach Gardens Police and a dispute with SunPass. A second invoice arrived anyway, and SunPass closed the dispute, but Keswick-Paine said she could not get confirmation the matter was resolved. By the time she reached out in April, she had received a third toll bill. She expressed concern about potential consequences, saying if someone runs a red light or hits and runs with the tag in her husband's name, it could create serious problems.

Personal injury attorney Doug Burnetti said temp tag fraud is far more common than many realize, noting that difficulty tracking the issue makes it attractive to criminals. A new Florida law that kicked in last year increased penalties for fraudulent temp tag use and made the tags easier for the state to track. Security consultant and retired police officer Gene Petrino recommended keeping thorough records of police reports and toll disputes. He advised people transitioning from temporary to permanent tags to either destroy the tag themselves or eliminate personal information before surrendering it to the tag agency.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound mom sets up Little Free Pantry to help neighbors with food costs
cards.teaser: Jacquelyn Koester placed a pantry stocked with food and baby essentials outside her home near the Hobe Sound Public Library to help families struggling with higher prices.
cards.body:
Jacquelyn Koester started a Little Free Pantry located just steps from her home behind the Hobe Sound Public Library to help neighbors cope with rising food and gas prices. The pantry stocks food and baby essentials for families in need with no questions asked. After posting a request for help on a Hobe Sound Facebook group, Koester said the community response was overwhelming, with donations regularly filling the shelves. She noted that when gas and food prices increased, the pantry was emptying faster than she could replace it.

The pantry has attracted support from beyond the immediate area. Someone posted anonymously in the Facebook group saying they drove up from Jupiter for the pantry and that it would help them get through their week. Koester said those messages keep her motivated to maintain the pantry and keep it accessible to anyone who needs it. She emphasized that the community's willingness to help demonstrates how people continue to support each other, even as communities change. For more information on how to access the pantry, residents can visit the Facebook group created by Koester.

cards.headline: Belle Glade residents discuss housing concerns at community meeting
cards.teaser: More than a dozen Belle Glade residents shared their stories at a Let's Hear It community meetup at the Belle Glade Library, covering topics from housing and affordability to local resources.
cards.body:
More than a dozen Belle Glade residents gathered at the Belle Glade Library during a Let's Hear It community meetup to discuss housing affordability and local resources. The conversation highlighted residents' concerns about homelessness in the area. Local activist Delories Butts asked why the community cannot help homeless people, while others shared their positive experiences living in Belle Glade. Resident Veronica Bain expressed her love for the community.

Lavita Holmes, executive director of Glades Lives Matter, described resources available to residents, including an ambassadorship program that selects three students from every school for year-long mentorship. The program holds students civically responsible for attending school board meetings and commission meetings while staying informed about their communities. The meeting also featured discussion of upcoming events, including the first Juneteenth pageant in the county's history, which will feature eight contestants in grades kindergarten through fifth grade, according to Codi Snead.

cards.headline: Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach ends youth supervision policy
cards.teaser: Rapids Water Park has ended its interim youth supervision policy that required guests ages 17 and younger to be accompanied by an adult chaperone.
cards.body:
Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach has ended its interim youth supervision policy, which required guests ages 17 and younger to be accompanied by an adult chaperone. The park said the policy was intermittent and pulled in and out based on work with local authorities and social media trends. It is no longer in effect.

In a statement, Tina Hatcher, representing the park, said the facility remains committed to providing a safe and family-friendly environment. While in effect, the policy required minors ages 17 and under to be accompanied by a parent, legal guardian, or other responsible adult who was at least 21 years old and had traveled to the park with the minor's group. Adult chaperones were required to present a valid government-issued ID showing both a photograph and date of birth upon entry, remain on-site for the duration of the visit, and were limited to supervising no more than five guests ages 17 and under per day. The park continues to uphold strict safety standards through its code of conduct, on-site police officers, and a visible security presence.

hero.headline: DEA's Miami drug lab analyzes 70% of all drugs seized nationwide, cocaine dominates
hero.teaser: The Drug Enforcement Administration's Southeast Regional Drug Laboratory in South Miami processes 70% of all drug evidence seized by the DEA nationwide.
hero.body:
Located behind iron gates in a South Miami industrial park, the Drug Enforcement Administration's Southeast Regional Drug Laboratory stands as the busiest DEA facility in the country. The lab receives approximately 70 percent of all drug evidence seized by the agency nationwide, a volume that reflects South Florida's critical role in the nation's drug supply chain. Allen Catterton, who has worked as a chemist for the DEA for 28 years, directs operations at the facility. The lab's 20 chemists analyze seized narcotics from the Southeast and Caribbean regions, with cocaine representing the dominant substance they encounter.

South Florida's geography makes it particularly vulnerable to drug trafficking. The region's coastal location and proximity to South America have established it as a major entry point for illegal drug smuggling, both by land and sea. This strategic positioning explains why cocaine remains the primary focus of the lab's work. Forensic chemists like Jenna Hamilton and Alyssa Sanchez spend their days testing seized drugs to determine their composition and verify their identity. Hamilton demonstrated the initial testing process for cocaine samples, using chemical solutions to identify substances. Last year, chemists at the lab testified in federal court approximately 152 times, translating their chemical findings into legal evidence.

The lab's mission has become increasingly complex as America's illegal drug supply evolves. Chemists now regularly encounter sophisticated synthetic opioids like fentanyl and carfentanil, a powerful animal tranquilizer that is exponentially more potent than fentanyl. One sample Sanchez analyzed contained roughly 16 percent fentanyl mixed with carfentanil, creating an extremely dangerous substance. To address these emerging threats, the lab has invested in advanced equipment including a Nuclear Magnetic Resonance machine that functions similarly to an MRI, breaking down unknown narcotics to the molecular level. According to Catterton, "We're constantly playing catch-up" as drug manufacturers continuously design new compounds intended to circumvent existing controlled substance laws.

The evidence vault currently stores approximately 50,000 pieces of evidence worth billions of dollars on the streets, with cocaine comprising most of the stockpile. Drugs remain in storage until their corresponding court cases conclude, a process that can extend from months to decades. Once cases close, the accumulated narcotics are destroyed in an incinerator. Last year alone, the facility incinerated roughly 300,000 pounds of drugs, averaging approximately 15 tons monthly. This behind-the-scenes operation represents a crucial but rarely publicized component of America's drug enforcement efforts, where scientific expertise works to understand and combat an ever-shifting black market that continues to claim lives.

She initiated the effort with a Facebook post, confident the community would respond. "I knew the second I posted on that group that Hobe Sound was going to show up for us because that's what we do, we are a tight knit community," Koester said. When gas and food prices increased, the pantry emptied faster than she could replenish it.

These messages motivate Koester to maintain the pantry and keep it accessible to anyone who needs it, no questions asked. "The saying it takes a village is so true and the villages look a lot different than they used to, but people still show up for each other and people want to help," she said. For more information on accessing the pantry, residents can visit the Facebook group created by Koester.

cards.headline: Martin County Sheriff's Office investigates fatal vehicle fire near Citrus Boulevard
cards.teaser: A fatal vehicle fire that initially appeared to be the result of a crash is now being investigated as a possible accidental ignition, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.
cards.body:
A fatal vehicle fire initially suspected to be crash-related is now being investigated as a possible accidental ignition, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. On Saturday just after 9 p.m., deputies and Martin County Fire Rescue responded to reports of a fully engulfed vehicle off the side of the road near Citrus Boulevard and Pineapple Court. When first responders arrived, they found the driver deceased inside the vehicle, burned beyond recognition.

Detectives initially treated the incident as a traffic crash-related fire but ruled out a collision as the cause after further investigation at the scene, prompting involvement of the agency's Criminal Investigations Division. Investigators now believe the fire may have started when the truck's exhaust ignited dry grass beneath the vehicle. For reasons still unknown, the driver was unable to escape the burning truck. Detectives have tentatively identified the victim and been in contact with family members. However, due to the condition of the remains, a positive identification cannot be made until DNA testing is completed, with results expected to take several weeks.

At Habitat for Humanity of Martin County, Executive Director Mike Readling reports an uptick in people seeking help with rent and bills, 95 percent of whom are renters. "The housing situation is so dire. It's gotten progressively worse. We have families coming in everyday," Readling said, noting the proposed tax cut would do little for the people his organization serves.

Attorney John Tolley says local governments facing revenue shortfalls could cut services, dip into reserves, or raise millage rates. If millage rates rise, homesteaded homeowners would still benefit from the tax break, according to realtor Michael Caputo. However, landlords who don't receive the exemption could face higher tax bills and pass those costs to renters, who aren't getting the tax break either. If passed, the amendment would lower the property tax cap on non-homesteaded properties, including commercial apartment complexes, from 10 percent down to 5 percent. Tolley suggested this could lead to lower rents, while Caputo predicted municipalities may not raise millage rates and the market may stabilize through supply and demand.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County deputy celebrating 30 years surprised by Vanilla Ice at awards ceremony
cards.teaser: A Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office deputy celebrating 30 years of service got an unexpected surprise at an awards ceremony: a visit from rapper Vanilla Ice.
cards.body:
Deputy Tina Izzarone was honored at the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office awards ceremony this month for celebrating 30 years of service. She received an unexpected surprise when rapper Vanilla Ice, whose real name is Rob Van Winkle, made a special appearance. The surprise was made possible by a young man named Raffie, whose connection to both the deputy and the rapper brought the moment together. The story began when Izzarone pulled Raffie's mother over for a traffic stop and noticed Raffie. "I noticed immediately of his specialness, and I made him feel really at ease knowing that his mother was not in trouble," Izzarone said.

Raffie remembered the deputy's kindness and approached her when they saw each other again a few months later. Raffie also has a longstanding friendship with Van Winkle. "Raffie and I go way back when he was a little kid and just a great honor to come out and do this," Van Winkle said. When Raffie and his mother planned to attend the awards ceremony, Raffie invited Van Winkle. The rapper and the deputy share the same birthday on October 31. Van Winkle described his bond with Raffie, noting he has a big monster truck that Raffie enjoys sitting in and using the air conditioner. As for Raffie's mother, she did receive a ticket from the traffic stop.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Library System launches summer reading challenge through July 31
cards.teaser: The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to Unearth a Story this summer as part of its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, running now through July 31.
cards.body:
The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to participate in its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, running through July 31. According to Community Engagement Manager Lindsey McMullen, the program offers free activities, incentives and grand prizes to encourage residents to rediscover the joy of reading. Participants can register at any library branch, complete an activity log and return it to claim a prize while supplies last. Returned logs also qualify readers for a drawing to win one of several grand prizes.

The challenge offers age-specific prizes. Children up to age 4 can take home a rubber duck. Kids ages 5 to 11 can choose from a fidget spinner, dinosaur-themed pop keychain or dino pencil. Teens ages 12 to 17 and adults can opt for a fidget spinner, chip clip or notebook. Each library branch is hosting special events ranging from children's story times and craft sessions to adult workshops and wellness programs. Families will also encounter Dewey the Library Owl and Penelope Rex, a dinosaur character, at various appearances throughout the challenge. According to the American Library Association, summertime reading programs help prevent the "summer slide" in student learning. The challenge is open to all county residents and library cardholders.

cards.headline: Humane Society of the Treasure Coast thrift stores in Stuart house adoptable cats during shelter renovation
cards.teaser: The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is using its two thrift stores to keep animal care going strong during a major renovation of its shelter in Palm City.
cards.body:
The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is using its two thrift stores as a temporary home for adoptable cats while its Palm City shelter undergoes major renovations. The nonprofit began construction on its adoption, customer service, and intake areas earlier this year, shifting many cats to the store locations, according to spokesperson Sarah Fisher. "With our shelter cages unavailable, the stores have become a lifeline for our animals," Fisher said Thursday.

Senior Manager Kelly Ellis said shoppers can now find adoptable cats alongside unique items for sale at both locations. "Every treasure you find here helps provide for our animals," Ellis noted, welcoming donations of gently used goods. The organization is also seeking temporary foster homes for other animals during the construction period. The thrift stores are located at 3302 SE Federal Highway in Stuart and 1099 NW 21st St, Stuart. Store hours and donation guidelines are available at hstc1.org.

cards.headline: Smithsonian Marine Exhibit in Fort Pierce showcases Florida ocean ecosystems with rare live displays
cards.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium invites visitors to explore Florida's coastal habitats through rare live encounters with marine life. Located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce's waterfront district, the facility has operated under the Smithsonian banner since 1980, displaying fully live, complex ecosystem models that set it apart from typical public aquariums. Manager Bill Hoffman noted that the facility houses more species than many larger exhibits around the country. The centerpiece is the Atlantic coral reef tank, which recreates one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems. Visitors also encounter live models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities, demonstrating intricate relationships between organisms, including the aquarium's four-inch barracuda. A touch tank allows guests to handle unusual marine species under staff supervision, often encountering animals they've never seen before.

The exhibit operates in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station to raise public awareness about ocean threats while inspiring conservation efforts. Hoffman emphasized that stable ecosystems depend on myriad small organisms, a message reinforced through the live displays. The facility is open to the public year-round, with upcoming programming planned to commemorate its 25th anniversary celebration. More information is available at sms.si.edu and on Smithsonian Marine Station social media channels.

hero.headline: Ron DeSantis says he's looking forward to private sector after leaving Florida Governor's Mansion
hero.body:
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said he plans to step away from politics after his term ends at the end of the year, though he continues to dodge direct questions about a potential 2028 presidential run. In recent comments, DeSantis acknowledged that many people want him to pursue different paths, but he emphasized his commitment to completing his current responsibilities. "I'm in my mid-40s, who knows what life will hold in the future? I have a lot of people that want me to do a lot of different things, but I think I owe it to the voters to just run through the tape here," he said. He expressed enthusiasm about returning to civilian life after his years in elected office and suggested the private sector may be where he focuses his attention next.

DeSantis acknowledged that his time as Governor has been an honor and pointed to accomplishments during his tenure. He indicated openness to pursuing private sector opportunities for a period before considering any future political moves. However, he stopped short of making any firm commitments about his long-term plans, leaving the door open for potential political activity down the road. He did promise that if he decides to make another political move, he would discuss it publicly.

Current polling data suggests limited appetite among Republican voters for a DeSantis presidential campaign. His strongest national poll performance showed him at 12 percent support among Republicans. State-level polling paints a bleaker picture, particularly in New Hampshire, a crucial early primary state, where he registered just 5 percent support. The political landscape has shifted considerably since his failed 2024 presidential campaign, with President Donald Trump actively promoting a ticket featuring Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Some political observers have drawn parallels between DeSantis's potential break from politics and Richard Nixon's decision to sit out the 1964 presidential race before mounting a successful comeback in 1968. Taking time away from the political spotlight could allow DeSantis to refresh his appeal to voters who may have grown weary of his profile. For now, DeSantis appears focused on finishing his governorship, which concludes at the end of 2026, before making any decisions about his political future.

cards.headline: Florida Attorney General Uthmeier sues TikTok over alleged violations of state law on minors
cards.teaser: Attorney General James Uthmeier filed a lawsuit Monday accusing TikTok of violating Florida law by allowing minors to access inappropriate content and deceiving parents.
cards.body:
Attorney General James Uthmeier sued TikTok on Monday, accusing the social media app of violating state law by permitting minors to view dangerous content. The lawsuit alleges that TikTok illegally allows children access to inappropriate material.

The complaint also accuses TikTok of deceiving parents about the content available to minors on the platform. The legal action represents the state's latest effort to regulate how social media companies interact with children and teenagers in Florida.

The lawsuit follows growing national concern about social media's impact on young users. Florida has passed several laws in recent years aimed at protecting minors online and holding tech companies accountable for content accessible to children.

cards.headline: Florida NOW PAC endorses Brandi Gabbard in St. Petersburg mayoral race
cards.teaser: The political arm of the National Organization for Women endorsed City Council member Brandi Gabbard for St. Petersburg mayor, citing her record on equality, environmental protection, and affordability.
cards.body:
The Florida NOW PAC has endorsed St. Petersburg City Council member Brandi Gabbard in her mayoral race against incumbent Mayor Ken Welch, former Gov. Charlie Crist, Kevin Batdorf, Jim Large, and Maria Scruggs. The statewide organization, which focuses on feminist advocacy, anti-discrimination efforts and equal rights for women, girls and nonbinary people, cited Gabbard's record on equality, justice, environmental protection and affordability. Ruth Whitney, a NOW member and St. Petersburg resident, said Gabbard has consistently demonstrated a strong commitment to NOW's core values.

Gabbard, a Realtor by trade, positions herself as a policy-focused candidate emphasizing her City Council record. Her platform includes exploring energy independence from Duke Energy, expanding access to missing middle housing, and reducing parking requirements to address affordability and high utility costs. The endorsement comes as St. Petersburg and other local governments prepare for new state restrictions on diversity, equity and inclusion programs. Gabbard said she is proud to receive the endorsement from a group with a strong track record of supporting qualified female candidates throughout Florida. If no candidate receives more than 50% of the vote, the top two finishers will advance to a November runoff.

cards.headline: Inside DEA's Miami lab, the busiest drug analysis facility in the nation
cards.teaser: The Drug Enforcement Administration's Southeast Regional Drug Laboratory in Miami processes 70% of all drug evidence seized by the DEA nationwide, with cocaine as the dominant substance.
cards.body:
The DEA's Southeast Regional Drug Laboratory in South Miami is the busiest drug analysis facility in the nation, processing approximately 70% of all drugs seized by the DEA nationwide by weight. Director Allen Catterton, a chemist with 28 years at the DEA, said the lab focuses on seized narcotics from the Southeast and the Caribbean. Lab staff provided about 152 testimonies in federal court last year. South Florida's coastal location and proximity to South America make it a top entry point for illegal drug smuggling.

The lab employs 20 chemists who analyze the makeup of drugs seized during investigations. Cocaine remains the dominant substance analyzed at the facility. The illegal drug supply is rapidly evolving, with deadlier substances appearing, including the synthetic opioid fentanyl and carfentanil, a large animal tranquilizer. One recent sample analyzed by chemist Alyssa Sanchez contained 16% fentanyl and carfentanil, which is multiple times more potent than fentanyl. The lab uses sophisticated equipment including a Nuclear Magnetic Resonance machine that functions like an MRI for unknown narcotics, breaking them down to the molecular level. The evidence vault currently stores about 50,000 pieces of evidence worth billions of dollars. Last year the lab destroyed roughly 300,000 pounds of drugs in an incinerator, approximately 15 tons per month.

cards.headline: Jenna Persons-Mulicka moves from writing Florida election laws to running Lee County elections
cards.teaser: Former state Rep. Jenna Persons-Mulicka, who carried high-profile election legislation in Tallahassee, now oversees elections in Lee County after Gov. DeSantis appointed her Supervisor of Elections in May.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed Jenna Persons-Mulicka as Lee County Supervisor of Elections in May to replace Tommy Doyle. The Fort Myers Republican spent six years in the Florida House as one of the GOP's leading voices on election legislation, carrying politically sensitive bills including voter citizenship verification, foreign influence legislation, and measures on constitutional amendments and congressional redistricting. She now implements the laws she helped write in one of Southwest Florida's largest counties. Persons-Mulicka described her transition from advocate to what she calls an "umpire" role.

Her early work as Supervisor of Elections has included reviewing voter-roll procedures, finalizing polling places, and returning a Dunbar voting site to the Dr. Carrie Robinson Center after hearing community concerns. The center, located in the historically minority-majority community of Fort Myers, had served as a traditional polling place for many years before Hurricane Ian forced a relocation. Her predecessor had planned to move the site elsewhere for this cycle before Persons-Mulicka reversed the decision. She was appointed just before candidate prequalifying started, and with qualifying now closed, she will oversee an election that includes her own name on the ballot in November. The Lee County office has received praise from state officials for maintaining one of Florida's most efficient petition verification processes.

cards.headline: Florida CFO Ingoglia announces arrests of 12 in public assistance fraud cases totaling $806,000
cards.teaser: The Department of Financial Services arrested 12 people in May for allegedly defrauding Florida public assistance programs of approximately $806,000 combined.
cards.body:
Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia announced that the Department of Financial Services Criminal Investigations Division arrested 12 people in May in connection with public assistance fraud cases involving approximately $806,000 combined in public assistance funding. Initially, the 12 people arrested were connected to $487,728 defrauded from public assistance programs. The Bureau of Public Assistance Fraud reviewed an additional 48 cases and found $318,895 in funding that was also allegedly defrauded. Ingoglia stated that Florida will continue to set the standard for cracking down on public assistance fraud and ensuring that criminals who engage in fraudulent schemes will face consequences.

Alexis Rivero was accused of the largest amount of fraud from the U.S. Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, more than $221,000, and is charged with public assistance fraud and grand theft. Other suspects arrested include Kristen Bowman, charged with public assistance fraud totaling $47,516.68; Nelida Reyes-Carrasquillo, charged with making false statements for public aid and grand theft totaling $42,113.46; David Jacobs, charged with public assistance fraud totaling $41,925.28; Karigan Burgos, charged with welfare fraud totaling $33,452.41; Janelle Josephik, charged with public assistance fraud totaling $32,662.90; Aurora Damian Chamu, charged with welfare fraud totaling $29,432.71; Yamalys Parrilla, charged with public assistance fraud totaling $18,123.78; Shlaberte Saintlouis, charged with public assistance fraud totaling $9,855; Ricki Ambrose, charged with public assistance fraud totaling $4,087.54; Carolyn Ruise, charged with welfare fraud totaling $3,964; and Tanya Yinger, charged with public assistance fraud totaling $2,806. Most arrestees have been disqualified from receiving SNAP benefits for at least a year, with some permanently disqualified.

cards.headline: The Southern Group expands Central Florida advocacy team with addition of Julian Cintron
cards.teaser: Lobbying firm The Southern Group added Orlando native Julian Cintron to its Orlando office, where he will focus on local government advocacy in Central Florida.
cards.body:
The Southern Group is expanding its Central Florida team with the addition of Julian Cintron to the firm's Orlando office. An Orlando native and former legislative staffer, Cintron will focus on local government advocacy, helping clients navigate policy, economic development, land-use and infrastructure issues before city councils, county commissions and regional governing bodies. Senior Managing Partner Rachel Cone said building out the local advocacy bench across the state has been a deliberate focus for the firm.

Prior to joining The Southern Group, Cintron worked for several Central Florida lawmakers, including Reps. Joy Goff-Marcil, Leonard Spencer and Anna Eskamani, as well as Sens. Carlos Guillermo Smith and Victor Torres. His legislative work included issues such as workforce development, artificial intelligence and transportation innovation. In addition to his legislative experience, Cintron helped lead Orlando YIMBY, a housing advocacy organization focused on land-use and growth policy issues. He also managed Spencer's successful 2024 campaign in House District 45, the only Democratic state House pickup in Florida that cycle. Sen. Torres said Cintron "knows how to work this process and build the relationships that get things done," while Rep. Eskamani called him "a proven advocate." Central Florida Market Lead Seth McKeel said the region continues to be one of the most dynamic in the state and clients need experienced advocates who understand the local governments driving that growth.

hero.headline: Hobe Sound mom starts Little Free Pantry to help neighbors cope with rising food costs
hero.body:
Jacquelyn Koester launched a Little Free Pantry outside her Hobe Sound home to help neighbors manage the impact of rising food and gas costs. What began as a simple Facebook post has grown into a community resource that provides basic necessities to anyone in need without judgment. The pantry, located behind the Hobe Sound Public Library, stocks food items and baby essentials for families facing financial hardship. "I knew the second I posted on that group that Hobe Sound was going to show up for us because that's what we do, we are a tight knit community," Koester said.

The pantry quickly became popular as families struggled with inflation. Koester found herself constantly restocking shelves as items disappeared rapidly. "When gas prices went up and food prices went up it was just emptying about faster than I can replace it," she explained. Rather than become discouraged, Koester turned to the community for support through a Facebook appeal. The response exceeded her expectations, with neighbors regularly donating items to keep the shelves stocked and available for those who needed assistance.

The impact of the pantry extended beyond her immediate neighborhood. One person anonymously posted in the Facebook group about traveling from Jupiter to access the pantry's resources. "Someone posted in the Facebook group anonymously saying I drove up from Jupiter for this, this is going to help get me through my week," Koester shared. These messages of gratitude and stories of genuine need reinforce her commitment to maintaining the pantry and ensuring it remains accessible to anyone in the community who requires help.

Koester reflects on how community support has evolved while remaining strong. She believes that while the methods of helping one another have changed, the underlying desire to support neighbors persists. "The saying it takes a village is so true and the villages look a lot different than they used to, but people still show up for each other and people want to help," she said. The pantry represents more than just a collection of donated items; it has become a symbol of community connection and mutual support during challenging economic times. For those interested in accessing the pantry or learning more about how to contribute, Koester maintains a Facebook group with information and updates about the initiative.

cards.headline: Fire near Newfield Parkway in Martin County extinguished with help from multiple agencies
cards.teaser: Multiple agencies responded to extinguish a fire near Newfield Parkway in Martin County.
cards.body:
Multiple fire agencies worked together to extinguish a fire near Newfield Parkway in Martin County. The fire required coordination between several responding agencies to bring under control.

The incident occurred near Newfield Parkway, requiring a multi-agency response. No further details about the cause of the fire or the extent of damage were provided in the report.

cards.headline: Driver found dead in burning vehicle in Martin County
cards.teaser: A driver was found dead inside a burning vehicle in Martin County. An investigation is ongoing.
cards.body:
A driver was found dead inside a burning vehicle in Martin County. The discovery was made when authorities responded to the scene of the vehicle fire.

Authorities are currently investigating the circumstances surrounding the death. The investigation remains ongoing to determine what led to the fire and the driver's death.

cards.headline: Two Martin County restaurants receive perfect inspection scores while one closed and three fail
cards.teaser: Two Martin County restaurants earned perfect scores in recent health inspections, but one was closed and three others failed.
cards.body:
Two restaurants in Martin County received perfect scores during recent health inspections. The restaurants met all requirements during their evaluations by health inspectors.

One Martin County restaurant was closed following its inspection. Three other restaurants in the county failed their health inspections, though specific details about the violations were not provided in the report.

cards.headline: 14-year-old Christopher Cetoute killed by speeding driver on North Congress Avenue in Boynton Beach
cards.teaser: Friends are mourning 14-year-old Christopher Cetoute, who was struck and killed by a speeding driver Friday night in Boynton Beach. A vigil will be held Friday at 7 p.m.
cards.body:
Friends of Christopher Cetoute are mourning the loss of the 14-year-old Congress Middle School student, who was fatally struck by a speeding driver Friday night along the 4600 block of North Congress Avenue in Boynton Beach. Boynton Beach police say Christopher was crossing the roadway going eastbound when he was struck by a 35-year-old driver traveling southbound. Police believe speeding played a factor, and Christopher was not crossing at a crosswalk. He was pronounced dead on scene.

Close friend Abrionna Lang remembered Christopher fondly. "To me CC was actually like a best friend," Lang said. "Loyal, hilarious, determined, caring, a sweet person. He was always easy to get close to." Friends described Christopher as someone who loved playing basketball and track. A memorial of flowers, a poster and a balloon now stands near the scene of the crash. A vigil will be held in Christopher's honor Friday at 7 p.m. at the memorial site on North Congress Avenue. No charges have been filed against the driver at this time.

cards.headline: Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach ends youth supervision policy requiring adult chaperones
cards.teaser: Rapids Water Park has ended its interim policy requiring guests ages 17 and younger to be accompanied by an adult chaperone.
cards.body:
Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach has ended its interim youth supervision policy, which required guests ages 17 and younger to be accompanied by an adult chaperone. The park said the policy was intermittent and pulled in and out based on work with local authorities and social media trends. It is no longer in effect.

While in effect, the policy required minors ages 17 and under to be accompanied by a parent, legal guardian or other responsible adult who was at least 21 years old and had traveled to the park with the minor's group. Adult chaperones were required to present a valid government-issued ID showing both a photograph and date of birth upon entry, remain on-site for the duration of the visit and were limited to supervising no more than five guests ages 17 and under per day. Guests can visit Rapids Water Park's website at rapidswaterpark.com for additional details before planning their visit.

cards.headline: Florida CFO Blaise Ingoglia to hold press conference in Boca Raton
cards.teaser: Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia will hold a press conference in Boca Raton this morning at 11 a.m.
cards.body: Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia will be holding a press conference in Boca Raton this morning at 11 a.m. WPTV will stream the press conference at 11 a.m.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County woman nearly loses over $400,000 to gold courier scam
hero.teaser: A St. Lucie County woman almost lost more than $400,000 to scammers using a gold courier scheme.
hero.body:
A woman in St. Lucie County came close to losing over $400,000 to criminals running a gold courier scam. The fraud scheme targets victims through deceptive tactics that convince them to convert their money into gold for pickup by couriers.

Gold courier scams typically involve criminals posing as government officials or law enforcement who convince victims their accounts are compromised. The scammers then direct victims to withdraw money, buy gold, and hand it over to a courier who claims to be securing the assets. Authorities are investigating the case involving the St. Lucie County woman.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie to distribute $24 million Waste Pro settlement via property tax roll
cards.teaser: Port St.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie city council voted Monday to distribute $24 million from a settlement with former trash hauler Waste Pro through the property tax roll rather than sending checks to residents. The tax roll option allows the city to distribute funds directly to properties using an established system. Council members also voted not to reimburse the city for prior emergency solid waste expenses in the general fund.

The settlement stems from trash collection problems during the pandemic when Waste Pro failed to pick up garbage, leaving overflowing bins on residents' yards. In 2021, both the company and city filed lawsuits against each other. Waste Pro blamed labor shortages while the city argued the company breached its contract for standard of service. The two parties reached the $24 million settlement agreement earlier this year. Resident Kelly Lee, who attended Monday's meeting, recalled neighbors' trash issues and questioned how the distribution would work fairly for residents who moved away since the service problems occurred. Scott Samples with the city said staff had been working to collect data and create scenarios to give recommendations to city council. Mayor Shannon Martin said in April after the settlement announcement that she wanted to see the cash in neighbors' pockets and was committed to making sure residents get paid back for what they dealt with during that time.

cards.headline: 18-year-old biking from Jacksonville to Keys missing, last seen in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: An 18-year-old bicycling from Jacksonville to the Florida Keys has been missing for several days after last being spotted in Fort Pierce.
cards.body:
Authorities are searching for an 18-year-old who has been missing for days while attempting to bike from Jacksonville to the Florida Keys. The teenager was last seen in Fort Pierce during the journey south.

The missing person was traveling the lengthy route by bicycle when contact was lost. Law enforcement agencies are working to locate the young traveler and determine their current whereabouts and condition.

cards.headline: Film 'As For Me & My House, Sundays Is For Church' to begin shooting in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: A new film production is scheduled to start filming in Fort Pierce on June 26.
cards.body:
The film 'As For Me & My House, Sundays Is For Church' is scheduled to begin filming on June 26 in Fort Pierce. Production will then move to Rockledge on June 27.

The Fort Pierce filming represents part of a multi-location shoot for the project. The production schedule calls for one day of filming in Fort Pierce before moving to the Brevard County location.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County labeled among riskiest areas for real estate in Florida
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County has been identified as one of the riskiest counties in Florida for real estate investments.
cards.body:
A new analysis has placed St. Lucie County among the riskiest areas in Florida for real estate. The county joins several other Florida locations on the list of markets facing elevated risk factors.

The designation reflects various factors that contribute to real estate risk in the area. St. Lucie County property owners and potential buyers face market conditions that analysts have flagged for heightened concern.

cards.headline: Six St. Lucie County restaurants earn perfect inspection scores while four fail
cards.teaser: Recent health inspections in St. Lucie County resulted in perfect scores for six restaurants and failures for four establishments.
cards.body:
Six restaurants in St. Lucie County received perfect scores during recent health inspections, while four other establishments failed to meet inspection standards. The inspections were conducted as part of regular health and safety reviews of food service locations.

The results show a mix of compliance levels among St. Lucie County dining establishments. Restaurants that failed inspections will need to address violations and undergo follow-up inspections to continue operating.

cards.headline: William A. Conticello Sr. of Port St. Lucie dies
cards.teaser: William A. Conticello Sr. of Port St. Lucie has died.
cards.body:
William A. Conticello Sr., a Port St. Lucie resident, has died. Funeral arrangements are being handled by Kent & Pelczar Funeral Home & Crematory.

Conticello's death was announced this week. Information about services is available through the funeral home.

hero.headline: Hobe Sound mom creates community food pantry to help neighbors fight rising grocery costs
hero.body:
Jacquelyn Koester saw her community struggling with rising food and gas prices, so she decided to take action. She started a Little Free Pantry outside her home, stocked with food and baby essentials for anyone in the Hobe Sound area who needs help. What began as a simple Facebook post to connect neighbors has grown into a reliable resource for families trying to make ends meet. The pantry operates on a no-questions-asked basis, ensuring that anyone facing financial hardship can access the supplies they need.

Located behind the Hobe Sound Public Library, the pantry has become a visible symbol of community care. Koester knew from the start that her neighbors would respond to the call for support. "I knew the second I posted on that group that Hobe Sound was going to show up for us because that's what we do, we are a tight knit community," she said. The community response exceeded her expectations, with donations regularly arriving to keep the shelves filled. The demand has been so high that Koester has struggled to restock items as quickly as they disappear. "When gas prices went up and food prices went up it was just emptying about faster than I can replace it," she said.

The pantry's impact extends beyond simple food distribution. Stories from people who have used the pantry reveal its real-world importance to struggling families. One person posted anonymously in the Facebook group that they drove from Jupiter specifically to access supplies from the pantry, saying it would help them get through the week. These messages from grateful community members keep Koester motivated to maintain the effort and ensure the pantry remains accessible to those who need it most.

Koester has created a Facebook group where residents can find information about accessing the pantry and learn how to contribute donations. She sees the pantry as more than just a charitable effort. It represents how communities continue to support one another through changing economic times. "The saying it takes a village is so true and the villages look a lot different than they used to, but people still show up for each other and people want to help," she said. What sits outside her home has become a steady stream of community support for families working to afford groceries in an environment of rising costs.

cards.headline: Vero Beach man charged in grandmother's murder as bodycam video shows tense arrest
cards.teaser: A Vero Beach man faces charges in his grandmother's murder. Law enforcement released bodycam footage showing the arrest.
cards.body:
Indian River County authorities arrested a Vero Beach man and charged him with murdering his grandmother. The arrest was captured on bodycam video that shows a tense confrontation between officers and the suspect.

The bodycam footage released by authorities documents the moments leading up to the arrest on Monday. Specific details about the victim and the circumstances of the killing were not provided in initial reports.

The case remains under investigation by local law enforcement. The suspect is being held as the criminal case moves forward through the court system.

cards.headline: Sebastian Police Chief Daniel Acosta retires as Tim Wood takes over as interim chief
cards.teaser: Sebastian Police Chief Daniel Acosta has retired from his position. Tim Wood was sworn in as interim chief to lead the department.
cards.body:
Sebastian Police Chief Daniel Acosta retired from his position leading the city's police department. The retirement marks the end of Acosta's tenure as the top law enforcement official in Sebastian.

Tim Wood was sworn in as the interim police chief following Acosta's departure. Wood will lead the Sebastian Police Department while the city determines its next steps for permanent leadership.

The transition took place on Tuesday. No additional details were provided about Acosta's years of service or Wood's background with the department.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie council votes to distribute $24 million Waste Pro settlement through tax roll
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie city council decided to distribute the $24 million Waste Pro settlement via the tax roll rather than sending checks.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie city council voted to distribute $24 million from a settlement with former trash hauler Waste Pro through the tax roll rather than sending individual checks to residents. The tax roll method allows the city to distribute funds directly to properties using an established system. Council members also voted against reimbursing the city for prior emergency solid waste expenses in the general fund.

The settlement stems from lawsuits filed in 2021 between the city and Waste Pro. The company blamed labor shortages while the city argued it was a breach of contract regarding service standards. Resident Kelly Lee recalled trash problems during the pandemic when Waste Pro failed to pick up waste. "It would just be a stinky mess on their yard," Lee said. "They didn't pick up, and it's overflowing." Scott Samples with the city said staff worked to collect data and create scenarios to help council make the distribution decision. "Ultimately the goal is to make the best decision possible, help remediate some of those issues, and those nightmares that people have from back then," Samples said.

cards.headline: Florida homestead exemption expansion could cost Martin County $67 million in revenue
cards.teaser: A proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could reduce Martin County's revenue by more than $67 million if approved by voters.
cards.body:
Rewritten Card Body

A proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could cost Martin County more than $67 million in revenue if approved by voters in November, according to a Florida Policy Institute analysis. Statewide, local governments could lose nearly $4.8 billion. The amendment would also lower the property tax cap on non-homesteaded properties, including commercial apartment complexes, from 10 percent down to 5 percent.

Attorney John Tolley said local governments facing revenue shortfalls would have limited options: cutting services, dipping into reserves, or raising millage rates. If rates rise, homesteaded homeowners would still benefit from the tax break, but landlords without the exemption could face higher bills and potentially pass those costs to renters. Mike Readling, executive director of Habitat for Humanity of Martin County, said 95 percent of people seeking help with rent and bills at his organization are renters. "The demographic that we're working with and Habitat for Humanity tries to help, it's not going to help them at all," Readling said. A 2025 Florida Senate analysis found just 24 affordable and available rental units for every 100 extremely low-income renters.

cards.headline: 14-year-old Congress Middle School student killed by speeding driver in Boynton Beach
cards.teaser: Christopher Cetoute, a 14-year-old Congress Middle School student, was fatally struck by a speeding driver on North Congress Avenue in Boynton Beach.
cards.body:
Christopher Cetoute, a 14-year-old student at Congress Middle School, was killed Friday night when struck by a speeding driver along the 4600 block of North Congress Avenue in Boynton Beach. According to Boynton Beach police, Christopher was crossing the roadway going eastbound when he was hit by a 35-year-old driver traveling southbound. Police believe speeding played a factor in the crash. Christopher was not crossing at a crosswalk and was pronounced dead at the scene. No charges have been filed against the driver at this time.

Friends remember Christopher as loyal, hilarious, determined, caring and easy to get close to. Abrionna Lang, a close friend, said "At first I didn't believe it until I'd seen a lot of stuff and then I just started crying. Like I was crying for the whole day." Christopher loved playing basketball and track. Caurline Robinson, who lives in the area, said she has witnessed at least seven crashes along Congress Avenue in the last eight years and is calling for safety enhancements. Robinson lost her 5-year-old great-grandchild to a speeding driver in 2021. A vigil will be held in Christopher's honor Friday at 7 p.m. at the memorial site on North Congress Avenue.

cards.headline: Belle Glade residents discuss housing concerns and community resources at library event
cards.teaser: More than a dozen Belle Glade residents gathered at the Belle Glade Library to share stories about housing affordability and local resources.
cards.body:
More than a dozen Belle Glade residents gathered at the Belle Glade Library during a Let's Hear It community meetup to discuss housing, affordability, local resources, and upcoming events. The conversation centered heavily on affordability and housing concerns. Local activist Delories Butts raised the question of why the community cannot help homeless people, while resident Veronica Bain expressed her appreciation for living in Belle Glade.

Lavita Holmes, executive director of Glades Lives Matter, highlighted an ambassadorship program that mentors three students from every school throughout the year. Holmes explained that the program holds students civically responsible for attending school board meetings and commission meetings while staying informed about their communities. She described the initiative as a voice for people residing in the Glades community. Codi Snead also announced the county's first Juneteenth pageant, featuring eight contestants from kindergarten through fifth grade. The Let's Hear It events focus on uncovering the real stories that make communities tick. Residents unable to attend monthly meetings can email LetsHearIt@wptv.com to share their concerns.
